prompt_spec.original_prompt:
The role of phantasia and Erschlossenheit in disclosing the environment:
how Aristotle's account of phantasia in De Anima III.3 anticipates
Heidegger's concept of disclosedness (Erschlossenheit) in Being and Time.

Specifically address:
(a) How Aristotle's phantasia functions as the faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena),
(b) How Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structures the disclosure of Being-in-the-world,
(c) The structural parallel between these two modes of disclosure,
(d) Where the two frameworks diverge — Aristotle's faculty psychology vs. Heidegger's existential analytic.

Include verbatim quotations from both De Anima and Being and Time.
Target length: 1000-1500 words. Write as a single coherent section suitable for a doctoral dissertation.

Where do Aristotle's faculty psychology and Heidegger's existential analytic diverge in their treatment of disclosure?

required_facets.name: Aristotle's Phantasia as Disclosure of Phainomena
required_facets.description: How does Aristotle theorize phantasia in De Anima Book III, Chapter 3 as the psychological faculty that mediates between perception (aisthesis) and thought (noesis), enabling the disclosure of appearances (phainomena) independently of immediate sensory presence? This facet investigates Aristotle's definition of phantasia as 'that in virtue of which an appearance comes about for us' (phantasia estin kath' hēn legomen phantasma ti hēmin gignesthai), examining how phantasia differs from both perception and belief (doxa), its role in making absent objects present to consciousness, and its function as a necessary condition for thought. The inquiry focuses on Aristotle's arguments that phantasia involves the capacity to apprehend appearances without the object being present, the relationship between phantasia and truth or falsity, and how this faculty structures our access to the world beyond immediate sensation.

required_facets.name: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit and Being-in-the-World
required_facets.description: How does Heidegger conceptualize Erschlossenheit (disclosedness) in Being and Time as the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's Being-in-the-world is opened up and made intelligible? This facet examines Heidegger's analysis of disclosedness as comprising three equiprimordial moments: Befindlichkeit (state-of-mind or attunement), Verstehen (understanding), and Rede (discourse), and how these constitute the 'there' (Da) of Dasein. The investigation focuses on Heidegger's claim that Dasein is its disclosedness, that disclosedness is more primordial than knowledge or perception, and how Erschlossenheit differs from epistemological theories of representation or mental states. Special attention is given to Heidegger's discussion in sections 28-34 and 44 of Being and Time, examining how disclosedness structures our pre-theoretical access to entities, the world, and ourselves, and how this relates to Heidegger's critique of the subject-object framework in traditional philosophy.

required_facets.name: Structural Parallels: Phantasia and Erschlossenheit
required_facets.description: What are the deep structural parallels between Aristotle's concept of phantasia and Heidegger's Erschlossenheit as modes of disclosure that mediate between immediate presence and interpretive understanding? This facet investigates how both concepts function as intermediary structures that enable access to what is not immediately present: phantasia making absent sensory objects available to thought, and Erschlossenheit opening up the totality of significance that constitutes the world. The inquiry examines whether both frameworks share a common concern with pre-predicative or pre-theoretical disclosure, how both resist reduction to either pure receptivity or pure spontaneity, and whether Heidegger's existential analytic can be read as a radicalization of Aristotelian insights about the mediating role of phantasia. This includes examining scholarly interpretations that trace Heidegger's phenomenological appropriation of Aristotelian psychology, particularly through the lens of medieval and phenomenological readings of De Anima.

required_facets.name: Divergence: Faculty Psychology vs. Existential Analytic
required_facets.description: Where and why do Aristotle's faculty psychology and Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverge in their treatment of disclosure, particularly regarding the ontological status of the disclosing structure and its relationship to human being? This facet examines the critical differences: Aristotle's phantasia as a psychological faculty possessed by the soul (psychē) within a substance-ontology framework versus Heidegger's Erschlossenheit as an existential structure constitutive of Dasein's very Being. The investigation focuses on how Aristotle maintains a representational model where phantasia produces mental images (phantasmata) that re-present absent objects, while Heidegger rejects representationalism in favor of a non-representational account of world-disclosure. This includes examining Heidegger's critique of traditional psychology and epistemology in Being and Time, his rejection of the subject-object schema, and how his existential-ontological approach transforms or abandons the Aristotelian framework of faculties, potentiality-actuality, and the soul as form of the body.

required_facets.name: Heidegger's Phenomenological Appropriation of Aristotle
required_facets.description: How does Heidegger's early engagement with Aristotle, particularly in his lecture courses of the 1920s and his phenomenological interpretation of Aristotelian texts, inform his development of the concept of Erschlossenheit and his broader existential analytic in Being and Time? This facet explores Heidegger's sustained dialogue with Aristotle throughout his early Freiburg and Marburg periods, examining how his phenomenological retrieval (Wiederholung) of Aristotelian concepts like alētheia, phainomena, logos, and kinēsis shaped his own philosophical vocabulary. The investigation includes Heidegger's lecture courses on Aristotle (particularly the 1924 Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy and the 1922 Phenomenological Interpretations of Aristotle), his interpretation of Aristotle's practical philosophy and its influence on his analysis of care (Sorge) and Being-in-the-world, and how Heidegger transforms Aristotelian insights while claiming to radicalize them phenomenologically.

claims.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses absent objects by making them present to consciousness without requiring their actual sensory presence, thereby establishing a mode of access to the world that transcends immediate perception.
grounds: Heidegger interprets Aristotelian thinking as involving 'φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's theory of phantasia 'attempts to deal with a large range of problems' concerning how consciousness accesses what is not immediately given in sensation.
The phantasma 'creates a certain impression' that differs from the eikōn or likeness, suggesting phantasia produces appearances rather than mere copies of sensory data.
claims.warrant: These textual elements demonstrate that phantasia operates as a distinctive cognitive capacity that bridges the gap between sensory absence and mental presence. By 'making-present-to-itself' what is not actually there, phantasia enables thought to operate on objects beyond immediate sensory contact, establishing a fundamental structure of disclosure that makes absent entities accessible to consciousness. This mediating function positions phantasia as more than mere image-production—it is a faculty that opens up a domain of appearances (phainomena) independent of direct perception.
claims.backing: Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle recognizes that phantasia addresses the fundamental problem of how consciousness relates to what is not immediately present, a concern central to phenomenological accounts of intentionality and world-disclosure.
claims.qualification: While Aristotle's account remains within a faculty psychology framework, the structural insight about mediated presence anticipates phenomenological concerns.

claims.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit constitutes the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's 'there' (Da) is opened up, establishing disclosedness as more primordial than any epistemological relation and as constitutive of Dasein's very Being rather than a property it possesses.
grounds: Heidegger emphasizes that 'If it lacks its "there", it is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all,' indicating that disclosedness is constitutive of Dasein's Being.

The analysis shows that 'the being-there of the human being was explicated as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in,' connecting disclosure to logos as fundamental structure.
Heidegger's interpretation reveals that 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading' in certain modes of disclosure, pointing to a pre-predicative access to beings.
claims.warrant: These passages establish that Erschlossenheit is not an epistemological capacity that Dasein possesses but rather the ontological structure that Dasein is. The 'there' (Da) of Dasein refers to the opened-up space of intelligibility within which entities can show themselves. Without this disclosedness, Dasein would not be the kind of entity it essentially is. This represents a radical departure from traditional theories of knowledge or mental representation, positioning disclosure as the condition for any possible relation to entities rather than as one cognitive function among others.
claims.backing: Heidegger's existential analytic transforms the question from 'how does a subject know objects?' to 'what is the Being of the entity for whom entities can be disclosed?' This ontological reorientation makes disclosedness fundamental to Dasein's existence.
claims.qualification: This claim reflects Heidegger's mature position in Being and Time, though his interpretation of Aristotle in the 1920s lectures shows the developmental trajectory of these ideas.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit constitutes the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's 'there' (Da) is opened up, establishing disclosedness as more primordial than any epistemological relation and as constitutive of Dasein's very Being rather than a property it possesses.

original_claim.warrant: These passages establish that Erschlossenheit is not an epistemological capacity that Dasein possesses but rather the ontological structure that Dasein is. The 'there' (Da) of Dasein refers to the opened-up space of intelligibility within which entities can show themselves. original_claim.backing: Heidegger's existential analytic transforms the question from 'how does a subject know objects?' to 'what is the Being of the entity for whom entities can be disclosed?' This ontological reorientation makes disclosedness fundamental to Dasein's existence.

original_claim.claim: Both phantasia and Erschlossenheit function as intermediary structures that enable access to what is not immediately present through a mode of disclosure that resists reduction to either pure receptivity or pure spontaneity, suggesting a structural parallel in their mediating roles.

Phantasia makes absent sensory objects available to thought by producing appearances that are neither mere sensations nor pure concepts. Similarly, Erschlossenheit opens up the world through an interpretive structure that is neither passive reception of data nor active construction of representations. Both operate in an intermediary space where the world becomes accessible through a structure that enables both truth and error, indicating genuine intentional directedness rather than mechanical causation or arbitrary invention.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's phenomenological appropriation of Aristotle suggests he recognized this structural affinity, even as he transformed the framework from faculty psychology to existential ontology. original_claim.warrant: These textual elements demonstrate that phantasia operates as a distinctive cognitive capacity that bridges the gap between sensory absence and mental presence. By 'making-present-to-itself' what is not actually there, phantasia enables thought to operate on objects beyond immediate sensory contact, establishing a fundamental structure of disclosure that makes absent entities accessible to consciousness. This mediating function positions phantasia as more than mere image-production—it is a faculty that opens up a domain of appearances (phainomena) independent of direct perception.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle recognizes that phantasia addresses the fundamental problem of how consciousness relates to what is not immediately present, a concern central to phenomenological accounts of intentionality and world-disclosure.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit constitutes the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's 'there' (Da) is opened up, establishing disclosedness as more primordial than any epistemological relation and as constitutive of Dasein's very Being rather than a property it possesses.
grounds: Heidegger emphasizes that 'If it lacks its "there", it is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all,' indicating that disclosedness is constitutive of Dasein's Being.

The analysis shows that 'the being-there of the human being was explicated as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in,' connecting disclosure to logos as fundamental structure.
Heidegger's interpretation reveals that 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading' in certain modes of disclosure, pointing to a pre-predicative access to beings.
original_claim.warrant: These passages establish that Erschlossenheit is not an epistemological capacity that Dasein possesses but rather the ontological structure that Dasein is. The 'there' (Da) of Dasein refers to the opened-up space of intelligibility within which entities can show themselves. Without this disclosedness, Dasein would not be the kind of entity it essentially is. This represents a radical departure from traditional theories of knowledge or mental representation, positioning disclosure as the condition for any possible relation to entities rather than as one cognitive function among others.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's existential analytic transforms the question from 'how does a subject know objects?' to 'what is the Being of the entity for whom entities can be disclosed?' This ontological reorientation makes disclosedness fundamental to Dasein's existence.
original_claim.qualification: This claim reflects Heidegger's mature position in Being and Time, though his interpretation of Aristotle in the 1920s lectures shows the developmental trajectory of these ideas.

original_claim.claim: Both phantasia and Erschlossenheit function as intermediary structures that enable access to what is not immediately present through a mode of disclosure that resists reduction to either pure receptivity or pure spontaneity, suggesting a structural parallel in their mediating roles.
grounds: Phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what 'is not actually there,' establishing a mode of presence-in-absence that mediates between sensation and thought.
Heidegger's analysis shows that being-in-the-world involves λόγος as 'the basic character' that structures disclosure, indicating a mediating interpretive dimension.

Both frameworks address how 'intentionality is required, one which makes error possible; and this requires its content to be explained in a different way,' pointing to a shared concern with non-immediate, mediated access to entities.
original_claim.warrant: The structural parallel emerges in how both concepts address the fundamental problem of mediated disclosure. Phantasia makes absent sensory objects available to thought by producing appearances that are neither mere sensations nor pure concepts. Similarly, Erschlossenheit opens up the world through an interpretive structure that is neither passive reception of data nor active construction of representations. Both operate in an intermediary space where the world becomes accessible through a structure that enables both truth and error, indicating genuine intentional directedness rather than mechanical causation or arbitrary invention.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's phenomenological appropriation of Aristotle suggests he recognized this structural affinity, even as he transformed the framework from faculty psychology to existential ontology. Both thinkers resist empiricist reduction of world-access to sensation and rationalist reduction to pure intellection.
original_claim.qualification: The parallel is structural rather than substantive—both address similar phenomenological problems while operating within fundamentally different ontological frameworks.
original_claim.rebuttal: Critics might argue that the parallel is superficial, given that Aristotle's phantasia produces mental images (phantasmata) while Heidegger explicitly rejects representationalism. However, the deeper structural similarity lies in the mediating function itself, not in the specific mechanism.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's faculty psychology and Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverge in their treatment of disclosure because Aristotle operates within a substance-ontology framework where phantasia is a capacity of the soul, while Heidegger rejects this framework entirely by making disclosedness constitutive of Dasein's Being rather than a property or faculty it possesses.
grounds: Aristotle's framework treats phantasia as addressing 'the τί ἤν εἶναι' which 'constitutes the particularity of beings,' operating within a substance-ontology that defines entities by their essential nature.

Heidegger emphasizes that without its 'there,' Dasein 'is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all,' making disclosedness ontologically constitutive rather than a possessed capacity.

The conceptual framework shows that 'Initially this conceptuality is not there in an original way; the possibilities of the conceptual are initially cut off by being-there,' indicating Heidegger's rejection of pre-given faculties in favor of existential structures.
original_claim.warrant: The divergence is ontological rather than merely terminological. Aristotle's phantasia operates within a framework where the soul (psychē) possesses various faculties (dynameis) that actualize potentialities according to the substance's essential nature. Phantasia is one such faculty—a capacity that the soul has. Heidegger's Erschlossenheit, by contrast, is not something Dasein has but what Dasein is. Disclosedness is not a property that could be added to or subtracted from an already-constituted subject; it is the very structure through which Dasein exists as the kind of being it is. This represents a fundamental shift from faculty psychology to existential ontology.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's critique of traditional psychology and epistemology in Being and Time explicitly targets the substance-ontology framework that treats mental capacities as properties of a subject-substance. His existential analytic dissolves the subject-object schema that underlies Aristotelian faculty psychology.
original_claim.qualification: Despite this fundamental divergence, Heidegger's engagement with Aristotle in his 1920s lectures suggests he saw his own project as radicalizing rather than simply rejecting Aristotelian insights.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might argue that Aristotle's hylomorphism already moves beyond crude substance-ontology by making form and matter inseparable. However, Aristotle still maintains the soul as the form of the body, preserving a substance-framework that Heidegger rejects.

The analysis emphasizes that in certain modes of disclosure 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading,' linking disclosure to alētheia as uncoveredness rather than correctness of representation.

Heidegger interprets Aristotelian concepts through the lens of presence and uncoveredness: 'Τοιόνδε, τοσόνδε, and so on: -δε proceeding from δή, "manifestly there," "present"—ways of being-present, by which the presence of beings themselves is determined.'
original_claim.warrant: Heidegger's appropriation of Aristotle involves a phenomenological retrieval (Wiederholung) that extracts insights about disclosure, presence, and uncoveredness from their original context in faculty psychology and reinterprets them as existential structures. By connecting logos to Being-in-the-world and alētheia to the uncoveredness of entities, Heidegger transforms Aristotelian concepts into elements of his existential analytic. This appropriation is not mere historical commentary but a philosophical transformation that claims to radicalize what was implicit in Aristotle by freeing it from the metaphysical framework of substance, form, and faculty.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's 1920s lecture courses on Aristotle demonstrate his sustained engagement with Aristotelian texts as resources for developing his own phenomenological ontology. His interpretation of Aristotelian concepts like kinēsis, energeia, and logos directly informed the development of Being and Time.
original_claim.qualification: Whether Heidegger's reading is faithful to Aristotle's original intentions remains contested among scholars, but the philosophical productivity of this appropriation is evident in the development of existential phenomenology.
original_claim.rebuttal: Critics might argue that Heidegger reads his own concerns back into Aristotle anachronistically. However, Heidegger's method of phenomenological retrieval explicitly aims to uncover possibilities in historical texts rather than to provide neutral historical reconstruction.

original_claim.claim: The divergence between Aristotle's representational model of phantasia, which produces mental images (phantasmata) that re-present absent objects, and Heidegger's non-representational account of world-disclosure reveals fundamentally different ontological commitments about how entities become accessible to understanding.
grounds: Aristotle's framework involves phantasia producing phantasmata that 'create a certain impression' distinct from direct likeness (eikōn), suggesting a representational intermediary between mind and world.

Heidegger's analysis emphasizes that disclosure operates through 'being-in-the-world' as a unitary structure rather than through mental representations, with 'λόγος' as 'the basic character' of this being-in.
The interpretive tradition shows that phantasia 'attempts to deal with a large range of problems' within a framework where mental contents mediate access to external reality.
original_claim.warrant: The representational versus non-representational divide marks a fundamental ontological difference. Aristotle's phantasia operates by producing mental images that stand in for absent sensory objects, maintaining a distinction between the mental representation and the external reality it represents. This preserves a subject-object framework where the mind contains representations of an external world. Heidegger's Erschlossenheit, by contrast, rejects this entire framework by arguing that Dasein is always already in-the-world, not as a subject confronting objects through representational intermediaries, but as a being whose very existence is constituted by its openness to entities. Disclosure is not mediated by mental representations but is the primordial structure through which entities show themselves.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's critique of representationalism in Being and Time targets the epistemological problems that arise from treating knowledge as a relation between mental representations and external objects. His existential analytic aims to show that this framework misconstrues the more primordial phenomenon of Being-in-the-world.
original_claim.qualification: Some interpreters argue that Aristotle's phantasia is less straightforwardly representational than traditional readings suggest, but the textual evidence supports a representational interpretation in which phantasmata function as mental intermediaries.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might object that Heidegger's account still involves a kind of 'representation' in the broad sense of making present. However, Heidegger's point is precisely that this making-present is not mediated by mental contents that stand between subject and object but is the primordial structure of Dasein's Being itself.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses absent objects by making them present to consciousness without requiring their actual sensory presence, thereby establishing a mode of access to the world that transcends immediate perception.
grounds: Heidegger interprets Aristotelian thinking as involving 'φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's theory of phantasia 'attempts to deal with a large range of problems' concerning how consciousness accesses what is not immediately given in sensation.
The phantasma 'creates a certain impression' that differs from the eikōn or likeness, suggesting phantasia produces appearances rather than mere copies of sensory data.
original_claim.warrant: These textual elements demonstrate that phantasia operates as a distinctive cognitive capacity that bridges the gap between sensory absence and mental presence. By 'making-present-to-itself' what is not actually there, phantasia enables thought to operate on objects beyond immediate sensory contact, establishing a fundamental structure of disclosure that makes absent entities accessible to consciousness. This mediating function positions phantasia as more than mere image-production—it is a faculty that opens up a domain of appearances (phainomena) independent of direct perception.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle recognizes that phantasia addresses the fundamental problem of how consciousness relates to what is not immediately present, a concern central to phenomenological accounts of intentionality and world-disclosure.
original_claim.qualification: While Aristotle's account remains within a faculty psychology framework, the structural insight about mediated presence anticipates phenomenological concerns.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit constitutes the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's 'there' (Da) is opened up, establishing disclosedness as more primordial than any epistemological relation and as constitutive of Dasein's very Being rather than a property it possesses.
grounds: Heidegger emphasizes that 'If it lacks its "there", it is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all,' indicating that disclosedness is constitutive of Dasein's Being.

The analysis shows that 'the being-there of the human being was explicated as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in,' connecting disclosure to logos as fundamental structure.
Heidegger's interpretation reveals that 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading' in certain modes of disclosure, pointing to a pre-predicative access to beings.
original_claim.warrant: These passages establish that Erschlossenheit is not an epistemological capacity that Dasein possesses but rather the ontological structure that Dasein is. The 'there' (Da) of Dasein refers to the opened-up space of intelligibility within which entities can show themselves. Without this disclosedness, Dasein would not be the kind of entity it essentially is. This represents a radical departure from traditional theories of knowledge or mental representation, positioning disclosure as the condition for any possible relation to entities rather than as one cognitive function among others.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's existential analytic transforms the question from 'how does a subject know objects?' to 'what is the Being of the entity for whom entities can be disclosed?' This ontological reorientation makes disclosedness fundamental to Dasein's existence.
original_claim.qualification: This claim reflects Heidegger's mature position in Being and Time, though his interpretation of Aristotle in the 1920s lectures shows the developmental trajectory of these ideas.

original_claim.claim: Both phantasia and Erschlossenheit function as intermediary structures that enable access to what is not immediately present through a mode of disclosure that resists reduction to either pure receptivity or pure spontaneity, suggesting a structural parallel in their mediating roles.
grounds: Phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what 'is not actually there,' establishing a mode of presence-in-absence that mediates between sensation and thought.
Heidegger's analysis shows that being-in-the-world involves λόγος as 'the basic character' that structures disclosure, indicating a mediating interpretive dimension.

Both frameworks address how 'intentionality is required, one which makes error possible; and this requires its content to be explained in a different way,' pointing to a shared concern with non-immediate, mediated access to entities.
original_claim.warrant: The structural parallel emerges in how both concepts address the fundamental problem of mediated disclosure. Phantasia makes absent sensory objects available to thought by producing appearances that are neither mere sensations nor pure concepts. Similarly, Erschlossenheit opens up the world through an interpretive structure that is neither passive reception of data nor active construction of representations. Both operate in an intermediary space where the world becomes accessible through a structure that enables both truth and error, indicating genuine intentional directedness rather than mechanical causation or arbitrary invention.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's phenomenological appropriation of Aristotle suggests he recognized this structural affinity, even as he transformed the framework from faculty psychology to existential ontology. Both thinkers resist empiricist reduction of world-access to sensation and rationalist reduction to pure intellection.
original_claim.qualification: The parallel is structural rather than substantive—both address similar phenomenological problems while operating within fundamentally different ontological frameworks.
original_claim.rebuttal: Critics might argue that the parallel is superficial, given that Aristotle's phantasia produces mental images (phantasmata) while Heidegger explicitly rejects representationalism. However, the deeper structural similarity lies in the mediating function itself, not in the specific mechanism.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's faculty psychology and Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverge in their treatment of disclosure because Aristotle operates within a substance-ontology framework where phantasia is a capacity of the soul, while Heidegger rejects this framework entirely by making disclosedness constitutive of Dasein's Being rather than a property or faculty it possesses.
grounds: Aristotle's framework treats phantasia as addressing 'the τί ἤν εἶναι' which 'constitutes the particularity of beings,' operating within a substance-ontology that defines entities by their essential nature.

Heidegger emphasizes that without its 'there,' Dasein 'is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all,' making disclosedness ontologically constitutive rather than a possessed capacity.

The conceptual framework shows that 'Initially this conceptuality is not there in an original way; the possibilities of the conceptual are initially cut off by being-there,' indicating Heidegger's rejection of pre-given faculties in favor of existential structures.
original_claim.warrant: The divergence is ontological rather than merely terminological. Aristotle's phantasia operates within a framework where the soul (psychē) possesses various faculties (dynameis) that actualize potentialities according to the substance's essential nature. Phantasia is one such faculty—a capacity that the soul has. Heidegger's Erschlossenheit, by contrast, is not something Dasein has but what Dasein is. Disclosedness is not a property that could be added to or subtracted from an already-constituted subject; it is the very structure through which Dasein exists as the kind of being it is. This represents a fundamental shift from faculty psychology to existential ontology.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's critique of traditional psychology and epistemology in Being and Time explicitly targets the substance-ontology framework that treats mental capacities as properties of a subject-substance. His existential analytic dissolves the subject-object schema that underlies Aristotelian faculty psychology.
original_claim.qualification: Despite this fundamental divergence, Heidegger's engagement with Aristotle in his 1920s lectures suggests he saw his own project as radicalizing rather than simply rejecting Aristotelian insights.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might argue that Aristotle's hylomorphism already moves beyond crude substance-ontology by making form and matter inseparable. However, Aristotle still maintains the soul as the form of the body, preserving a substance-framework that Heidegger rejects.

original_claim.claim: The divergence between Aristotle's representational model of phantasia, which produces mental images (phantasmata) that re-present absent objects, and Heidegger's non-representational account of world-disclosure reveals fundamentally different ontological commitments about how entities become accessible to understanding.
grounds: Aristotle's framework involves phantasia producing phantasmata that 'create a certain impression' distinct from direct likeness (eikōn), suggesting a representational intermediary between mind and world.

Heidegger's analysis emphasizes that disclosure operates through 'being-in-the-world' as a unitary structure rather than through mental representations, with 'λόγος' as 'the basic character' of this being-in.
The interpretive tradition shows that phantasia 'attempts to deal with a large range of problems' within a framework where mental contents mediate access to external reality.
original_claim.warrant: The representational versus non-representational divide marks a fundamental ontological difference. Aristotle's phantasia operates by producing mental images that stand in for absent sensory objects, maintaining a distinction between the mental representation and the external reality it represents. This preserves a subject-object framework where the mind contains representations of an external world. Heidegger's Erschlossenheit, by contrast, rejects this entire framework by arguing that Dasein is always already in-the-world, not as a subject confronting objects through representational intermediaries, but as a being whose very existence is constituted by its openness to entities. Disclosure is not mediated by mental representations but is the primordial structure through which entities show themselves.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's critique of representationalism in Being and Time targets the epistemological problems that arise from treating knowledge as a relation between mental representations and external objects. His existential analytic aims to show that this framework misconstrues the more primordial phenomenon of Being-in-the-world.
original_claim.qualification: Some interpreters argue that Aristotle's phantasia is less straightforwardly representational than traditional readings suggest, but the textual evidence supports a representational interpretation in which phantasmata function as mental intermediaries.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might object that Heidegger's account still involves a kind of 'representation' in the broad sense of making present. However, Heidegger's point is precisely that this making-present is not mediated by mental contents that stand between subject and object but is the primordial structure of Dasein's Being itself.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses absent objects by making them present to consciousness without requiring their actual sensory presence, thereby establishing a mode of access to the world that transcends immediate perception.
grounds: Heidegger interprets Aristotelian thinking as involving 'φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's theory of phantasia 'attempts to deal with a large range of problems' concerning how consciousness accesses what is not immediately given in sensation.
The phantasma 'creates a certain impression' that differs from the eikōn or likeness, suggesting phantasia produces appearances rather than mere copies of sensory data.
original_claim.warrant: These textual elements demonstrate that phantasia operates as a distinctive cognitive capacity that bridges the gap between sensory absence and mental presence. By 'making-present-to-itself' what is not actually there, phantasia enables thought to operate on objects beyond immediate sensory contact, establishing a fundamental structure of disclosure that makes absent entities accessible to consciousness. This mediating function positions phantasia as more than mere image-production—it is a faculty that opens up a domain of appearances (phainomena) independent of direct perception.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle recognizes that phantasia addresses the fundamental problem of how consciousness relates to what is not immediately present, a concern central to phenomenological accounts of intentionality and world-disclosure.
original_claim.qualification: While Aristotle's account remains within a faculty psychology framework, the structural insight about mediated presence anticipates phenomenological concerns.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit constitutes the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's 'there' (Da) is opened up, establishing disclosedness as more primordial than any epistemological relation and as constitutive of Dasein's very Being rather than a property it possesses.
grounds: Heidegger emphasizes that 'If it lacks its "there", it is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all,' indicating that disclosedness is constitutive of Dasein's Being.

The analysis shows that 'the being-there of the human being was explicated as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in,' connecting disclosure to logos as fundamental structure.
Heidegger's interpretation reveals that 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading' in certain modes of disclosure, pointing to a pre-predicative access to beings.
original_claim.warrant: These passages establish that Erschlossenheit is not an epistemological capacity that Dasein possesses but rather the ontological structure that Dasein is. The 'there' (Da) of Dasein refers to the opened-up space of intelligibility within which entities can show themselves. Without this disclosedness, Dasein would not be the kind of entity it essentially is. This represents a radical departure from traditional theories of knowledge or mental representation, positioning disclosure as the condition for any possible relation to entities rather than as one cognitive function among others.
original_claim.backing: Heidegger's existential analytic transforms the question from 'how does a subject know objects?' to 'what is the Being of the entity for whom entities can be disclosed?' This ontological reorientation makes disclosedness fundamental to Dasein's existence.
original_claim.qualification: This claim reflects Heidegger's mature position in Being and Time, though his interpretation of Aristotle in the 1920s lectures shows the developmental trajectory of these ideas.

This mediating function subsequently positions phantasia as more than mere image-production—it is a faculty that opens up a domain of appearances independent of direct perception, hence constituting a necessary condition for cognitive activity that extends beyond the spatiotemporal constraints of immediate sensory experience.

While Aristotle's account remains within a faculty psychology framework, the structural insight about mediated presence anticipates phenomenological concerns that reach their fullest articulation in Heidegger's ontological reformulation of disclosure. Heidegger's Erschlossenheit constitutes the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's 'there' (Da) is opened up, establishing disclosedness as more primordial than any epistemological relation and as constitutive of Dasein's very Being rather than a property it possesses. Heidegger emphasizes that "if it lacks its 'there', it is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all," indicating that disclosedness is constitutive of Dasein's Being rather than an attribute that might contingently belong to it. Furthermore, the analysis shows that "the being-there of the human being was explicated as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in," connecting disclosure to logos as fundamental structure. These passages establish that Erschlossenheit is not an epistemological capacity that Dasein possesses but rather the ontological structure that Dasein is, whereby the 'there' (Da) of Dasein refers to the opened-up space of intelligibility within which entities can show themselves. Without this disclosedness, Dasein would not be the kind of entity it essentially is, and this represents a radical departure from traditional theories of knowledge or mental representation, positioning disclosure as the condition for any possible relation to entities rather than as one cognitive function among others.

The structural parallels between phantasia and Erschlossenheit become most evident when we recognize that both function as intermediary structures enabling access to what is not immediately present through a mode of disclosure that resists reduction to either pure receptivity or pure spontaneity. Phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what 'is not actually there,' establishing a mode of presence-in-absence that mediates between sensation and thought, while Heidegger's analysis demonstrates that being-in-the-world involves λόγος as 'the basic character' that structures disclosure, indicating a mediating interpretive dimension that similarly transcends the dichotomy between passive reception and active construction. Both frameworks address how 'intentionality is required, one which makes error possible; and this requires its content to be explained in a different way,' pointing to a shared concern with non-immediate, mediated access to entities that cannot be adequately captured by models of direct sensory apprehension or purely conceptual determination. This claim reflects Heidegger's mature position in Being and Time, though his interpretation of Aristotle in the 1920s lectures shows the developmental trajectory of these ideas, revealing how his engagement with phantasia's mediating structure informed his articulation of Erschlossenheit as the ontological condition for Dasein's access to entities through modes of disclosure that are neither purely given nor purely constructed.

The structural parallel emerges in how both concepts address the fundamental problem of mediated disclosure, though this parallel remains structural rather than substantive, as both address similar phenomenological problems while operating within fundamentally different ontological frameworks. Phantasia makes absent sensory objects available to thought by producing appearances that are neither mere sensations nor pure concepts, establishing a mediating capacity that enables cognitive access to what is not immediately present through sensory channels. Erschlossenheit, in a structurally analogous manner, opens up the world through an interpretive structure that is neither passive reception of data nor active construction of representations, constituting instead the ontological condition for Dasein's engagement with entities in their being. Both operate in an intermediary space where the world becomes accessible through a structure that enables both truth and error, indicating genuine intentional directedness rather than mechanical causation or arbitrary invention, thereby revealing that disclosure requires a mediating dimension that transcends the traditional epistemological dichotomy between receptivity and spontaneity. Heidegger, by contrast, rejects this entire framework by making disclosedness constitutive of Dasein's Being itself rather than a faculty it possesses, emphasizing that without its 'there,' Dasein 'is not factically the entity which is essentially Dasein; indeed, it is not this entity at all,' such that the structure of Erschlossenheit cannot be understood as an attribute inhering in a substance but must be grasped as the ontological condition for Dasein's existence as such. Despite this fundamental divergence, however, Heidegger's sustained engagement with Aristotle in his 1920s lectures suggests he saw his own project as radicalizing rather than simply rejecting Aristotelian insights, thereby indicating that the movement from faculty to existential structure represents a retrieval and transformation of Greek ontology rather than its wholesale abandonment.

Heidegger's phenomenological retrieval of Aristotle effects a radical transformation of disclosure by repositioning logos and alētheia as fundamental structures of Being-in-the-world rather than as epistemological mechanisms operating within a representational framework. His lectures demonstrate that "being-there of the human being was explicated as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being," thereby establishing logos not as a faculty of judgment or propositional assertion but as the constitutive articulation through which Dasein's existential situation becomes intelligible. By anchoring logos in Being-in-the-world and reinterpreting alētheia as the uncoveredness of entities rather than as a property of propositions, Heidegger systematically transforms Aristotelian concepts into constitutive elements of his existential analytic, thereby claiming to radicalize what remained implicit in Aristotle by liberating these insights from the metaphysical apparatus of substance, form, and faculty that had subsequently enclosed them. Nonetheless, the philosophical productivity of this hermeneutic engagement proves undeniable in the subsequent development of existential phenomenology, insofar as Heidegger's Aristotelian retrieval provides conceptual resources for articulating pre-theoretical disclosure, temporal ekstasis, and the priority of practical comportment over theoretical representation, thereby establishing a methodological paradigm that extends far beyond questions of historical fidelity to shape twentieth-century Continental philosophy's understanding of intentionality, worldhood, and interpretive understanding.

The divergence between Aristotle's representational model of phantasia, which produces mental images (phantasmata) that re-present absent objects, and Heidegger's non-representational account of world-disclosure reveals fundamentally different ontological commitments about how entities become accessible to understanding. Within Aristotle's framework, phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that produces phantasmata which "create a certain impression" distinct from direct likeness (eikōn), thereby suggesting a representational intermediary between mind and world that enables thought to operate upon absent objects through internally generated images. The interpretive tradition demonstrates that phantasia "attempts to deal with a large range of problems" concerning perception, memory, and conceptual thought, all within a framework where mental contents necessarily mediate cognitive access to external reality, establishing a subject-object division that subsequent epistemology would inherit and systematize. Heidegger's analysis, by contrast, emphasizes that disclosure operates through "being-in-the-world" as a unitary structure rather than through mental representations, with "λόγος" serving as "the basic character" of this being-in, thereby precluding any mediating layer of phantasmata between Dasein and the entities it encounters. This fundamental opposition between representational and non-representational models of access crystallizes the broader philosophical stakes of Heidegger's retrieval, insofar as his rejection of phantasia as a mediating faculty constitutes a systematic dismantling of the epistemological problematic that has dominated Western philosophy since Descartes, replacing questions of how internal representations correspond to external objects with an investigation of the prior conditions that make entities show up as intelligible within a disclosed world.

The representational versus non-representational divide marks a fundamental ontological difference that structures the entire philosophical distance between Aristotle's phantasia and Heidegger's Erschlossenheit, insofar as this divide determines not merely how cognition operates but what sort of being the cognitive agent is. Aristotle's phantasia operates by producing mental images that stand in for absent sensory objects, maintaining a distinction between the mental representation and the external reality it represents, thereby preserving a subject-object framework where the mind contains representations of an external world that exist as intermediaries between the perceiving subject and the perceived entities. Heidegger's Erschlossenheit, by contrast, rejects this entire framework by arguing that Dasein is always already in-the-world, not as a subject confronting objects through representational intermediaries, but as a being whose very existence is constituted by its openness to entities, such that disclosure is not mediated by mental representations but is the primordial structure through which entities show themselves in their intelligibility. Hence the Aristotelian framework remains committed to a mediational structure that Heidegger's phenomenology systematically dismantles by locating intelligibility not in mental contents but in the disclosive structure of being-in-the-world itself.
